name: Design a Continuous Profiling Platform
intent: Profile every process in a large fleet all the time at a tiny cost, and let engineers see which code burns the CPU, compare two releases and trace it back to a service.
codeTitle: stack interning, flame graphs and a release diff
finalIntro: One profile from a running service, from a sample to a flame graph diff.
prompt: Design a continuous profiling platform for a company with 5,000 hosts running about 30,000 processes in Go, Java, Python and C++. Engineers want an always-on view of where CPU time goes, flame graphs for any service and time range, a comparison of two releases, and the profiling itself must never hurt production.
functional: Collect CPU (and later memory and lock) profiles from every process, all the time
Show a flame graph for any service, tag set and time range
Turn raw addresses into function names and line numbers
Compare two time ranges or two releases and show what got slower
Attribute cost to services, versions, hosts and custom tags such as endpoint or tenant
Control the sampling rate and the overhead per service, and switch profiling off in one step
nonFunctional: Profiling costs under 1% of a core in each process, and never blocks the application
About 600,000 samples per second across the fleet, with ingest bandwidth in the low megabytes per second
A flame graph for one service over an hour appears in a few seconds
Keep 30 days of profiles at a storage cost that is small compared with the CPU the fleet uses
A crashed collector or symbol service loses at most a few minutes of data and never affects the applications
Profiles contain code paths and tags, so access follows the access rules for the service

firstAttempt.text: When there is an incident, an engineer logs into one server, attaches a profiler such as perf or pprof for 30 seconds, and saves the flame graph as an SVG. To compare, they profile another server by hand and look at the two pictures.
limits: The slow moment is usually over by the time someone attaches, so the evidence is gone
A profile of one process for 30 seconds is a tiny and noisy sample of a fleet of 30,000
Attaching a heavy profiler to a struggling production process can make it worse
Symbols live on the build machines, so the SVG often shows hex addresses
There is no history, so a regression from last Tuesday's release cannot be compared with anything

steps.title: Put a low-overhead sampling agent in every process
steps.problem: Profiling by hand misses the incident, covers one process, and a heavy profiler can hurt the process it is meant to help.
steps.fix: Run a sampler all the time. Instead of tracing every call, it wakes up about 20 to 100 times per second, records the call stack of the code that is running right now, and goes back to sleep. In Go the runtime does this with a timer signal, on Java an agent uses the JVM's stack-walking interface, and on Linux an eBPF program can sample native code in every process without changing it. Each sample is a list of return addresses with a count, so the cost is a few microseconds to a few hundred, and the total is a small fixed fraction of a core. The agent keeps counts in memory and uploads them once a minute to an ingest gateway, which authenticates it and tags the data with the service, version, host and region.
steps.tradeoff: Overhead stays tiny and nearly constant, and nothing needs a restart. Sampling is statistical, so a function that runs for a very short time may never be seen in one profile, and the timer must not tick in lockstep with the work, or it will always see the same moment.

steps.title: Aggregate stacks and send them through a queue
steps.problem: Shipping every raw sample means 600,000 stacks per second of about 336 bytes each, around 200 MB/s, and the same few hundred stacks repeat over and over.
steps.fix: Stacks repeat, so count them. The agent folds identical stacks into one entry with a count, and gives each stack an id that is a hash (for example a 64-bit hash of its frames). After the first upload it sends only the id and the count for stacks the server already knows, and the full stack just for new ones. That shrinks the traffic from about 200 MB/s to a few MB/s. The ingest gateway writes the uploads to a queue, and stack aggregators read from it, merge uploads and drop duplicates when an agent retries.
steps.tradeoff: Traffic and storage drop by well over an order of magnitude, and the agents are decoupled from slow storage. Individual samples lose their exact time within the minute, and the agent and the aggregator must agree on how stacks are hashed, or the same stack gets two ids.

steps.title: Symbolise addresses into function names
steps.problem: A sampler sees return addresses like 0x4a91f0, which tell nobody anything, and the debug symbols are far too big to ship with each process.
steps.fix: Each upload names the binary by its build id, and the address is stored as an offset inside that binary. A symbolizer service looks the build id up in a symbol store, filled by the build pipeline with the debug information of every released binary, and turns each offset into a function, file and line, including inlined functions. Because stacks are deduplicated, each unique address is resolved once and cached. For languages with a runtime, such as Java and Python, the agent already supplies names, and the symbolizer only handles native code.
steps.tradeoff: Agents stay small and fast, and old releases can still be read months later. The symbol store grows with every build and must not lose a release, and a build whose symbols were never uploaded shows up as unresolved addresses, which must be shown as such rather than hidden.

steps.title: Store profiles as compressed blocks with a stack table
steps.problem: 10 billion rows per day cannot sit in a general database, and queries cover many services, tags and weeks.
steps.fix: Keep two things. A stack table stores each distinct stack once, as a list of frame ids, and a frame table stores each function once. The samples are tiny rows of series (the service and its tags), minute, stack id and count, which are grouped into blocks per time window and written as columns. Timestamps use delta encoding, stack ids are dictionary-coded and counts use variable-length integers, and a general compressor such as zstd on top gives roughly 5 times. A tag index maps service, version and region to the series that carry them, so a query reads only the blocks it needs. Blocks are immutable files in object storage, with recent ones also in memory. Old data is rolled up: after a week, per-minute counts are merged into hourly ones.
steps.tradeoff: A month of profiles for a large fleet fits in under a terabyte, and queries read only the columns they need. Compression and block building add a delay of a few minutes before data is final, and high-cardinality tags such as user id would explode the number of series.

steps.title: Serve flame graphs, merges and diffs
steps.problem: Engineers ask for any service, any tag and any time range, and above all they ask what changed between two releases.
steps.fix: A query selects the series by tags and time, reads the blocks, and merges the stacks by adding counts. A flame graph is made by building a tree over the frames: each node's width is the number of samples whose stack starts with that path. A diff turns two ranges, or two versions, into two trees and compares each node's share of its own total rather than its raw count, because the two ranges may have a different number of samples. The result is coloured by the change. The same query can group by tag, such as endpoint or tenant, to attribute cost, and results for popular queries are cached.
steps.tradeoff: Regressions are found in seconds and attributed to code and owners. Merging many hours of many processes is real work, so queries are limited and parallel, and a diff of tiny services is noisy because there are too few samples.

steps.title: Control overhead and sampling rate centrally
steps.problem: Profiling is only acceptable if it is guaranteed cheap, and a bug or a hot loop in the profiler must never take the application down.
steps.fix: Agents ask a rate controller for their settings. Each service has an overhead budget, for example 1% of a core, and a base rate. The agent measures its own cost per sample and chooses the highest rate that stays inside the budget, with a hard cap. The controller lowers rates under load or when the ingest is behind, raises the rate for a service during an investigation, and has a kill switch per service and per fleet that agents poll every few seconds. Agents also use jitter, so they do not all sample or upload at the same moment, and they drop data rather than block when the network is slow.
steps.tradeoff: The platform has a stated worst case, and operators can switch it off in seconds. A lower rate means fewer samples per function, so small functions become hard to see, and the controller is one more piece of infrastructure that must fail open with safe defaults.

failures.scenario: The sampler ticks in lockstep with the application
failures.impact: A loop of 10 ms sampled by a fixed 100 Hz timer is always seen at the same point, so a function that really takes 30% of the time shows as 0% or 100%.
failures.answer: Randomise the interval between samples around the target rate, and start timers at a random phase. Pick rates that are not round numbers, such as 19 or 97 Hz. Merging many processes also averages the bias out, which is a good reason to profile a whole service rather than one process.

failures.scenario: Symbols are missing for a release
failures.impact: Flame graphs for that version show raw addresses, and a diff against the previous version compares unnamed blocks.
failures.answer: Show unresolved frames as their binary and offset, and keep the raw stacks so they can be symbolised later. The deploy pipeline refuses to promote a build whose symbols are not in the store, and an alert fires when the share of unresolved samples for a service rises.

failures.scenario: The ingest path falls behind after a deploy restarts every process
failures.impact: 30,000 agents start with empty stack caches and upload full stacks together, so traffic jumps many times above normal.
failures.answer: Agents add random jitter before the first upload and send only new stacks in full. The gateway sheds load with an explicit retry-after, agents drop data older than a few minutes instead of queueing without limit, and the queue absorbs the rest. A short gap in profiles is acceptable, and slowing the application is not.

failures.scenario: A profiling agent itself misbehaves in production
failures.impact: A bug makes the sampler spin, or a high rate on a busy service costs 5% of its CPU and raises latency.
failures.answer: The agent watches its own CPU time and lowers its rate, and past a hard limit stops itself. The rate controller can disable one service or the whole fleet within a few seconds, and defaults to a low safe rate if it cannot be reached. New agent versions roll out as a canary to a few percent of hosts first.

failures.scenario: A tag with too many values is added
failures.impact: Someone tags profiles with the request id, so the number of series grows with the traffic and the index and the blocks explode.
failures.answer: Tags have an allow-list and a limit on distinct values per tag. Excess values are folded into an 'other' bucket, an alert reports series growth, and the agent drops a tag that exceeds its limit. For individual requests, a tracing system links to one profile instead.

alternatives.title: How to sample

options.name: Timer-based sampling in the runtime or agent
options.pro: Cheap and works for any language the runtime supports
options.con: Needs a per-language agent, and timers can align with the work

options.name: eBPF sampling from the kernel
options.pro: One agent for every process, with no changes or restarts
options.con: Needs a modern kernel and privileges, and managed-language frames need extra help

options.name: Instrumentation or tracing of every call
options.con: Slows the program, often a lot, and cannot be left on

alternatives.pick: Timer or eBPF sampling for always-on CPU profiles. Reserve tracing for short, targeted investigations.

alternatives.title: Where stacks are deduplicated

options.name: In the agent, with stack ids and counts
options.pro: Cuts network traffic by far the most
options.con: Agent and server must agree on the hashing and a cache protocol

options.name: On the server only
options.con: Pays the whole network cost of raw samples

options.name: Only at query time
options.con: Storage and reads are many times larger

alternatives.pick: Dedup in the agent and again in the store, since the stack table makes both cheap.

alternatives.title: When to symbolise

options.name: At ingest
options.pro: Stored data is readable, and queries are simple
options.con: Needs symbols the moment a build is deployed, and mistakes are stored

options.name: At query time
options.pro: Raw data can be fixed later, and missing symbols can be added afterwards
options.con: Every query pays for symbolising, though caches help

alternatives.pick: Store addresses and build ids, and symbolise at query time with a cache, so symbols can arrive late.

alternatives.title: How long to keep detail

options.name: Full resolution for 30 days
options.pro: Any question can be answered precisely

options.name: Full for a week, then hourly roll-ups
options.pro: Far fewer rows for older data
options.con: Cannot look at one-minute detail from last month

alternatives.pick: Roll up after a week. Keep the profiles around a released version's rollout longer, since regressions are compared against them.

roles.label: Engineers
roles.description: People who look at flame graphs and compare releases.

roles.label: Entry points
roles.description: The ingest gateway and the query API.

roles.label: Sample queue
roles.description: Uploaded profile data waiting to be aggregated.

roles.label: Processing
roles.description: Sampling agents, aggregation, symbolization, diffing and rate control.

roles.label: State
roles.description: Symbols, compressed profile blocks and the tag index.

quiz.question: A checkout service had a 4-minute latency spike yesterday. The on-call engineer logged in to one host after the page and ran a 30-second profile, which showed nothing unusual. What change would make the cause findable next time?
options: Write a runbook so that the on-call engineer attaches the profiler within one minute of the alert, on the three busiest hosts
Run a sampler in every process all the time, 20 to 100 times a second, and keep the stacks as history
Trace every function call in every process and store the full traces, so that nothing is missed in a spike
Extend the manual profile to 10 minutes and run it on a larger set of hosts after each page
quiz.explanation: The evidence is gone by the time a person attaches, so profiling has to be always on and cheap, which sampling 20 to 100 times a second gives. A faster runbook still arrives after the spike. Tracing every call costs far too much to leave on in production.

quiz.question: A fleet produces 600,000 samples a second, and each raw sample is a stack of about 336 bytes, which is around 200 MB/s. Most samples repeat the same few hundred stacks. Which change cuts the network traffic the most?
options: Compress each raw sample with zstd before it leaves the host, which saves roughly 5 times on the wire and needs no protocol change
Send the raw samples unchanged and let the server deduplicate them before it writes them to storage, so agents stay trivial
Halve the sampling rate on every host, which halves the bytes sent while the flame graph shapes stay the same
Let the agent fold identical stacks into one entry with a count, and send only the stack id and count once the server already knows the stack
quiz.explanation: Folding in the agent turns a repeat into a short id plus a count, which takes the traffic from about 200 MB/s to a few MB/s. Compression alone still leaves about 40 MB/s. Server-side dedup pays the whole network cost first, and halving the rate loses detail for only a 2 times gain.

quiz.question: A single Java process runs a request loop that takes exactly 10 ms, and a fixed 100 Hz sampler is the only profile source. A function that really uses 30% of each loop shows up as 0% in one profile and 100% in the next. What is the most direct fix?
options: Randomise the sample gaps and timer phase
Raise the rate to 1,000 Hz, so there are ten times more samples inside every loop of the process
Switch to tracing so that every call is counted exactly, and keep it on permanently in the process
Lower the rate to 50 Hz, so that the sampler is less likely to hit the same point of the loop twice in a row
quiz.explanation: The timer is locked in step with the work, so it keeps seeing the same moment. Random gaps and phase, with a rate such as 97 Hz, break that lock. A rate of 1,000 Hz or 50 Hz is still a multiple of the loop period and so stays aligned, while 1,000 Hz also costs ten times more.
